Thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap and agreed next steps on the data/privacy side so we have the same picture:

- Your ask: for PHI-adjacent PII fields we should not persist raw user inputs at all (effectively 0-retention for those tokens).
- Primary use case: live inference for patient triage flows; audit logs are required but must not contain raw PII.
- Constraints: your legal team needs evidence of immutable audit logs for compliance, and SecOps needs the ability to trace requests for incidents without seeing PII.

Next steps we agreed on the call:

2) Monica from CS will validate operational impact and run a small test in our sandbox.
3) HealthSecure will share the formal data handling spreadsheet you mentioned (please attach).

I’ve attached the demo recording and our SOC2 summary for your security team to review.

Proposed timeline: initial technical options by EOD Mon (Mar 8), sandbox test week of Mar 15. Does that work?

Priyom —

Appreciate the recap. A couple clarifications from our security/legal side:

- When we say 0-retention for PII we mean that for a defined set of attributes (name, MRN, SSN, full DOB, phone, email) we must not persist raw tokens in any logs, cache, or monitoring buckets.
- However we still need an immutable audit trail that indicates a request occurred (time, route, user id hash) plus a hashed fingerprint of the payload for deduping, but that fingerprint must not be reversible.
- We also need an option where certain non-PII metadata (region, model-version, latency buckets) are retained for 90 days for analytics.

Is it possible to support: (A) zero raw retention for specified fields at request time, (B) generation of a non-reversible payload fingerprint, and (C) a separate analytics log that omits PII and is TTL-based?

I’ve attached the spreadsheet you requested (healthsecure-data-requirements.xlsx). Can you include a short proposal for how Redwood would implement the above and any operational trade-offs?

Thanks,
Jane Smith
Director, Security & Compliance
HealthSecure Inc.

Hi Jane —

Thanks for the spreadsheet and the specific asks. Looping in Marcus (legal) and Monica (CS/devops) to validate feasibility and note any contractual/operational constraints.

Short answer (summary):
- Option 1 — Zero-data mode (strict): requests are processed in-memory; KV cache and prefix caches are disabled for the named PII fields; no raw tokens are written to logs, and we do not persist any reconstruction artifacts. We can emit an immutable byte-level audit record that contains only: timestamp, route id, model id, request fingerprint (SHA-256 of normalized payload), and an internal non-reversible request id. This meets the 0-retention requirement but has trade-offs: no replayability for debugging and slightly higher latency due to disabled caching.

- Option 2 — Masked retention: redact PII fields at ingestion (token-level replacement), keep a reversible but encrypted mapping in a customer-managed KMS if you want future rehydration. This would not be 0-retention; it is useful for debugging and would require KMS / contract clauses.

- Option 3 — Analytics-only logs: emit a separate analytics stream that never contains PII (we can configure which fields), retained for a TTL (we suggest 90 days).

Operational impacts:
- Zero-data mode requires a configuration flag per route and per-model. It is available to Dedicated and Private customers as a configuration we can enforce. For Hosted customers it’s subject to platform controls; we can scope to HealthSecure under a Dedicated commitment or an Enterprise Private deployment.
- SLA impact: if caching is disabled broadly, you may see 5–12% higher median latency on conversational flows. We’ll quantify with a small sandbox run.

Action items I’ll take:
- Monica to run a sandbox test (Mar 15–19) and capture latency + error delta.
- Marcus to draft a contractual exception language for 0-retention (to be reviewed by your legal).
- I’ll prepare a one-page options table and a short risk matrix by EOD Wed (Mar 10).

—Priyom

Hi team —

I ran an initial smoke in our internal sandbox today using a route-config prototype. Notes:

- We can implement a per-route "zero-data" flag that strips designated PII fields before any cache/write. Verified for both prefix cache and KV cache.
- We emit a request fingerprint (SHA-256) and a non-reversible request-id. The fingerprint is computed after deterministic normalization (lowercase, whitespace collapse).
- Analytics stream: we can pipeline a separate log that contains model version, latency_ms bucket, region, and hashed user-id; TTL is configurable (90/180/365 days).

Trade-offs observed:
- Median latency increase: ~8% at 128-token median; peak p90 increases about 15% in our small test.
- Debugging on production-only events will require a special rehydration path (customer-managed KMS) if you want reversible mappings.

I'll schedule a brief sandbox demo and produce the CSV with latency samples. If HealthSecure wants to proceed with Zero-data in Hosted, we will need an exception in our standard data retention policy and a signed addendum. Marcus, can you draft the addendum language?

Thanks,
Monica Patel
Principal Customer Engineer
Redwood Inference

Jane —

Following up on the legal side. Attached is a draft addendum that codifies a Zero-Data Mode exception for specified PII fields for the HealthSecure account under Redwood’s Hosted API, subject to the following high-level conditions: 

1) HealthSecure must provide a definitive list of attributes to be treated as PII (the spreadsheet you shared is a good start).
2) Redwood will provide an immutable audit record (timestamp, route, model, non-reversible request id, fingerprint as SHA-256). That fingerprint is explicitly defined as non-reversible and will be used only for deduping and incident correlation.
3) HealthSecure will accept operational caveats: measurable latency delta (as Monica documented) and a limited debugging posture (no raw replay).
4) The exception will be scoped to routes specified in the addendum and subject to quarterly review.

If this looks reasonable we can move to a redline pass. I’ve also included an appendix that lists the technical controls and a sample logging schema.

Marcus Lin
Senior Counsel, Privacy & Security
Redwood Inference
